simple: the information in front of the data that tells the network and the receiver how to handle it.
analogy: the outside of the envelope and the numbers in the corner.
precise: a sequence of fields of fixed size and position at the start of a packet, defined by a protocol specification; each field has a byte offset, a width and a byte order.
source: D1 of F5-01 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (packet switching, best effort), the link layer (MTU, loopback) and IP) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the data the packet is carrying for someone.
analogy: the letter inside the envelope.
precise: the bytes of a packet after its header; the protocol that built the header does not interpret them.
source: D1 of F5-01 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (packet switching, best effort), the link layer (MTU, loopback) and IP) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the network tries to deliver each packet, but promises nothing.
analogy: the post usually works, but cards can be late, lost, doubled or overtaken.
precise: a service model in which packets may be lost, duplicated, reordered, delayed or damaged, and the sender is not told; the Internet Protocol provides this service and leaves reliability to higher layers.
source: D2 of F5-01 (IETF RFC 791, "Internet Protocol" (DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification), sections on the overview of operation (best-effort, unreliable service), the header format (field order, network byte order, header checksum, time to live) and fragmentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the agreed order of the bytes of a number on the wire: most significant byte first.
analogy: both towns agree to write numbers left to right, biggest digit first.
precise: big-endian order, which the Internet protocol specifications use for multi-byte header fields; a little-endian machine must convert (SP201 F2-18 defined endianness).
source: D2 of F5-01 (IETF RFC 791, "Internet Protocol" (DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification), sections on the overview of operation (best-effort, unreliable service), the header format (field order, network byte order, header checksum, time to live) and fragmentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small number computed from the data, sent with it, so the receiver can notice damage.
analogy: the letter count written at the bottom of the card.
precise: a value computed over a block of bytes by a fixed rule; the Internet checksum is the 16-bit ones' complement of the ones' complement sum of the 16-bit words. It detects many, but not all, errors.
source: D3 of F5-01 (IETF RFC 1071, "Computing the Internet Checksum": the ones' complement sum, its properties and its limits) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the biggest packet one kind of link will carry.
analogy: the largest envelope the post van accepts.
precise: the largest packet, in bytes, that a network interface sends without splitting it; the value depends on the link type and configuration.
source: D1 of F5-01 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (packet switching, best effort), the link layer (MTU, loopback) and IP) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a pretend network inside one computer: packets sent to it come straight back to the same machine.
analogy: a letter you post to your own house.
precise: a software network interface (named lo on Linux) holding the address 127.0.0.1; packets sent to it are delivered to the same host without leaving it.
source: D1 of F5-01 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (packet switching, best effort), the link layer (MTU, loopback) and IP) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one job of the network, done by one protocol, using only the job below it.
analogy: the van driver, the post office, the family at the door: each handles only its own label.
precise: a level in a protocol architecture; a layer offers a service to the layer above and uses the service of the layer below, and talks to its peer layer on the other machine through its own header.
source: D1 of F5-02 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (layering, encapsulation, demultiplexing), the link layer and IP (checksum offload, segmentation offload, middle boxes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: putting one layer's packet, header and all, inside the next layer's packet as its payload.
analogy: the envelope goes into the bag, the bag onto the van.
precise: the process in which each layer on the sending side prepends its header (and sometimes appends a trailer) to the data unit it received from the layer above.
source: D1 of F5-02 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (layering, encapsulation, demultiplexing), the link layer and IP (checksum offload, segmentation offload, middle boxes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: on arrival, choosing who gets the packet next by reading one field of the current header.
analogy: the family reads the name on the envelope to decide who opens it.
precise: the receiving side's use of a field in each header — EtherType, then the IP protocol number, then the destination port — to select the next protocol or the receiving socket.
source: D1 of F5-02 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (layering, encapsulation, demultiplexing), the link layer and IP (checksum offload, segmentation offload, middle boxes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the name for a packet at the link layer, the one that travels on one wire.
analogy: the van with its label.
precise: the link-layer data unit; for Ethernet, destination and source MAC addresses, an EtherType and the payload (on the wire also a preamble and a frame check sequence that captures usually omit).
source: D5 of F5-02 (IEEE 802.3, "IEEE Standard for Ethernet", clauses on the MAC frame format (preamble, addresses, type field, frame check sequence)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a 16-bit number that says which program on a computer a packet is for.
analogy: the name of the person in the house.
precise: a 16-bit field in the UDP and TCP headers; the destination port, together with the address and protocol, selects the receiving socket. Not the same as a Verilog port (HW201) or an x86 I/O port (HW204).
source: D3 of F5-02 (IETF RFC 768, "User Datagram Protocol": ports, length, checksum and pseudo-header) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a few fields borrowed from the IP header and included in the UDP or TCP checksum, but never sent as part of the UDP or TCP header.
analogy: Kofi's family checks that the house address on the bag matches their house before trusting the envelope.
precise: source address, destination address, protocol number and transport length, prepended only for the checksum computation, so that a datagram delivered to the wrong address fails the check.
source: D3 of F5-02 (IETF RFC 768, "User Datagram Protocol": ports, length, checksum and pseudo-header) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: letting the network card compute a checksum instead of the CPU.
analogy: the van driver adds the count at the bottom, so the copy kept at the office has a blank.
precise: a feature where the operating system leaves a checksum incomplete and the network interface finishes it while sending; captures taken on the sending host then show a value that is not the final one.
source: D1 of F5-02 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the introduction (layering, encapsulation, demultiplexing), the link layer and IP (checksum offload, segmentation offload, middle boxes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a frame for every machine on the link.
analogy: calling out along the whole street.
precise: a frame whose destination MAC address is all ones, ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff; every interface on the link accepts it.
source: D5 of F5-03 (IEEE 802.3, "IEEE Standard for Ethernet", MAC frame format and address fields; IEEE 802, "Overview and Architecture", for the individual/group and universal/local address bits) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a 32-bit number that identifies an interface across the whole internet, written as four numbers 0–255 with dots.
analogy: the full postal address: street and house.
precise: a 32-bit value carried in the IPv4 header; in dotted-decimal notation each of the four bytes, most significant first, is written in decimal.
source: D2 of F5-03 (IETF RFC 791, "Internet Protocol", sections on addressing and the header's address fields) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many leading bits of an address name the network; the rest name the host.
analogy: the rule saying which part of the address is "the street".
precise: a prefix length n (written /n) means the first n bits are the network part; the subnet mask is the 32-bit value with n ones followed by 32 − n zeros, so that address AND mask = network address.
source: D6 of F5-03 (IETF RFC 4632, "Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan": prefixes, masks, longest-match forwarding) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a group of addresses that share the same network part and sit on the same link.
analogy: one street.
precise: the set of addresses with a given prefix; hosts in the same subnet reach each other directly at the link layer, without a router.
source: D1 of F5-03 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the link layer (switches, promiscuous mode), Internet addresses (subnets, CIDR, special addresses), ARP and IP forwarding) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the router a host sends everything to that is not on its own subnet.
analogy: the street's post office.
precise: the next hop of the route 0.0.0.0/0, the least specific route, used when no more specific route matches.
source: D1 of F5-03 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols" (second edition), chapters on the link layer (switches, promiscuous mode), Internet addresses (subnets, CIDR, special addresses), ARP and IP forwarding) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when several routes fit a destination, use the most specific one.
analogy: "River Street, house 15" beats "River Street" beats "anywhere".
precise: the IPv4 forwarding rule that selects, among table entries whose prefix matches the destination, the entry with the largest prefix length.
source: D6 of F5-03 (IETF RFC 4632, "Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan": prefixes, masks, longest-match forwarding) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the way a host finds the MAC address that belongs to an IPv4 address on its own link.
analogy: calling out "who lives at number 77?" and getting an answer.
precise: a protocol carried directly in Ethernet frames (its own EtherType): a broadcast request "who has address X? tell Y" and a unicast reply "X is at MAC M"; hosts cache the answers.
source: D3 of F5-03 (IETF RFC 826, "An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol": packet format, request and reply, cache) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a transport protocol that sends separate messages with no connection and no guarantees.
analogy: postcards.
precise: a transport protocol that adds ports, a length and an optional checksum to IP; each send is one datagram and each receive returns one whole datagram; no delivery, ordering or duplicate protection.
source: D3 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 768, "User Datagram Protocol") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a transport protocol that gives two programs a reliable, ordered stream of bytes.
analogy: the numbered story with receipts.
precise: a connection-oriented transport protocol providing a reliable, in-order, full-duplex byte stream with flow control and congestion control, built on IP datagrams.
source: D2 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (replaces RFC 793): sections on the header format, sequence numbers, establishing a connection, closing a connection, data communication (retransmission, window management), the state machine and resets) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one TCP packet.
analogy: one page of the story.
precise: the TCP data unit: a TCP header (ports, sequence number, acknowledgment number, flags, window, checksum, options) and zero or more bytes of the stream.
source: D2 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (replaces RFC 793): sections on the header format, sequence numbers, establishing a connection, closing a connection, data communication (retransmission, window management), the state machine and resets) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: numbers that count bytes, so each side knows exactly which bytes were sent and received.
analogy: page numbers, and the receipt "I have everything before page n".
precise: the sequence number is the stream position of a segment's first byte (SYN and FIN each count as one); the acknowledgment number is the next byte the sender of the ACK expects, which confirms every byte before it.
source: D2 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (replaces RFC 793): sections on the header format, sequence numbers, establishing a connection, closing a connection, data communication (retransmission, window management), the state machine and resets) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the three packets that open a TCP connection.
analogy: "shall we start?", "yes, shall we?", "yes".
precise: SYN (client's initial sequence number), SYN-ACK (server's initial sequence number and acknowledgment of the client's), ACK; options such as the maximum segment size and window scaling are agreed here.
source: D2 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (replaces RFC 793): sections on the header format, sequence numbers, establishing a connection, closing a connection, data communication (retransmission, window management), the state machine and resets) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many more bytes the receiver can accept right now.
analogy: how many pages still fit in the mailbox.
precise: the window field of each segment advertises the amount of buffer space the receiver has free beyond the acknowledged byte; the sender may not have more unacknowledged data than that in flight. A zero window stops the sender.
source: D2 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (replaces RFC 793): sections on the header format, sequence numbers, establishing a connection, closing a connection, data communication (retransmission, window management), the state machine and resets) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: sending data again because it was not acknowledged.
analogy: copying a page again when no receipt came.
precise: TCP resends unacknowledged data when its retransmission timer expires, or earlier when duplicate acknowledgments or selective acknowledgments indicate a loss (fast retransmit).
source: D2 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (replaces RFC 793): sections on the header format, sequence numbers, establishing a connection, closing a connection, data communication (retransmission, window management), the state machine and resets) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the sender slowing itself down so it does not overload the network between the two ends.
analogy: not posting more pages than the post office can carry this week.
precise: algorithms that limit the sender's data in flight by a congestion window, which grows while data is acknowledged and shrinks when loss (or other signals) indicates congestion; the sender uses the smaller of the congestion window and the receive window.
source: D5 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 5681, "TCP Congestion Control" (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: IP's error-report messages.
analogy: the post office's "addressee unknown" slip.
precise: a protocol carried in IP datagrams that reports errors such as "destination unreachable (port unreachable)" back to the source.
source: D4 of F5-04 (IETF RFC 792, "Internet Control Message Protocol": destination unreachable messages and their codes) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the program's end of a network conversation, used like a file.
analogy: a mailbox slot in your house wall that only your program uses.
precise: a kernel object created by socket() and referred to by a file descriptor; it has a type (stream for TCP, datagram for UDP), local and remote addresses, and kernel send and receive buffers.
source: D1 of F5-05 (W. Richard Stevens, Bill Fenner and Andrew M. Rudoff, "UNIX Network Programming, Volume 1: The Sockets Networking API" (third edition), chapters on elementary TCP sockets, I/O multiplexing (select and poll), and socket options) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a socket that waits for new TCP connections instead of carrying data.
analogy: the receptionist who greets callers and hands each one to a new desk.
precise: a stream socket on which listen() was called; the kernel completes handshakes and queues connections, and each accept() returns a new, connected socket for one of them.
source: D2 of F5-05 (The Open Group Base Specifications (POSIX.1), pages for getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo, gai_strerror, socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, shutdown, close, poll, setsockopt) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the library call that turns a host name and a port into addresses you can connect to.
analogy: looking up a friend's address before writing.
precise: the POSIX function that resolves a node name and a service into a linked list of socket addresses (IPv4 and IPv6), freed with freeaddrinfo; errors are reported as its own codes, turned into text by gai_strerror.
source: D2 of F5-05 (The Open Group Base Specifications (POSIX.1), pages for getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo, gai_strerror, socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, shutdown, close, poll, setsockopt) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: send and recv may move fewer bytes than you asked for.
analogy: the van takes only the pages that fit; you collect only the pages already in the tray.
precise: on a stream socket, send returns the number of bytes accepted and recv the number of bytes available, each possibly less than requested; correct code loops.
source: D2 of F5-05 (The Open Group Base Specifications (POSIX.1), pages for getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo, gai_strerror, socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, shutdown, close, poll, setsockopt) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: marking where each message starts and ends inside a byte stream.
analogy: writing "this letter has 3 pages" on the first page.
precise: an application-level convention, such as a fixed-size length prefix or a delimiter, that lets the receiver split a TCP byte stream back into messages.
source: D4 of F5-05 (Bjarne Stroustrup, "A Tour of C++" (edition to be recorded), chapters on resource management and move semantics; C++ Core Guidelines, resource-management rules) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one thread that waits until any of many sockets is ready, then handles only what is ready.
analogy: Jun looks at all his trays at once and works on whichever has something to do.
precise: a loop around poll(), which blocks until at least one of the given file descriptors is readable or writable (or has an error) and reports which; the program then performs operations that will not block.
source: D2 of F5-05 (The Open Group Base Specifications (POSIX.1), pages for getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo, gai_strerror, socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, shutdown, close, poll, setsockopt) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: saying "I will send nothing more" while still listening for the answer.
analogy: "that was my last page; I am still reading yours".
precise: shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) sends a FIN for one direction (F5-04) while the socket can still receive; the peer's recv then returns 0 after the last byte.
source: D2 of F5-05 (The Open Group Base Specifications (POSIX.1), pages for getaddrinfo, freeaddrinfo, gai_strerror, socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, shutdown, close, poll, setsockopt) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the internet's address book, turning names into addresses.
analogy: the town's address book.
precise: a distributed, hierarchical database of resource records, queried with a request–response protocol, usually one UDP datagram each way on port 53 (TCP for large answers).
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a name like web.lab.example, read from right to left as ever smaller areas.
analogy: "the copy shop, river town, valley country".
precise: a sequence of labels (each at most 63 bytes), written with dots and encoded on the wire as length-prefixed labels ending in a zero byte.
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the software that asks DNS questions for programs.
analogy: the helper who looks up the book for you.
precise: a stub resolver in the C library sends queries to the servers listed in its configuration (on Linux, /etc/resolv.conf); a recursive resolver answers them by querying authoritative servers from the root down, and caches the answers.
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the server that holds the official data for one part of the name space.
analogy: the town hall that keeps its own town's book.
precise: a server loaded with a zone's records; its answers carry the AA (authoritative answer) flag.
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one entry in DNS, for example "this name has this IPv4 address".
analogy: one line in the address book.
precise: name, type, class, TTL and data; type A (1) carries a 4-byte IPv4 address, AAAA an IPv6 address, CNAME an alias, MX a mail server, NS a name server.
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long an answer may be kept and reused.
analogy: "this entry is good for five minutes; then look again".
precise: a 32-bit count of seconds in every record that bounds how long resolvers may cache it; not the same as the IPv4 header's TTL (F5-03), which counts router hops.
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the DNS answer "this name does not exist".
analogy: "no such name in this town".
precise: response code 3 (Name Error) from an authoritative source; the C library reports it to programs as "Name or service not known" on Linux in this build.
source: D1 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities", and RFC 1035, "Domain Names — Implementation and Specification" (message format, labels, compression, header flags, response codes, record types, TTL, UDP 512-byte limit)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how a computer joining a network gets an IP address and settings automatically.
analogy: the town hall that lends a newcomer a house number.
precise: a UDP protocol (client port 68, server port 67) built on BOOTP; a client broadcasts Discover, servers Offer an address, the client Requests one, and the server acknowledges (ACK), with options such as subnet mask, router and DNS servers.
source: D2 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 2131, "Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol" (messages, ports, lease, renewal times)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the time for which an address is lent.
analogy: "you may use number 57 for an hour".
precise: the duration in option 51; the client renews before it ends and must stop using the address if it cannot.
source: D2 of F5-06 (IETF RFC 2131, "Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol" (messages, ports, lease, renewal times)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long one message takes to get where it is going.
analogy: how long one letter takes to arrive.
precise: the time from sending a message to its arrival (one-way) or to the arrival of its reply (round trip); it includes processing in both hosts, queueing, transmission and propagation, and varies from message to message.
source: D1 of F5-07 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1" (second edition), chapters on TCP data flow, window management and performance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the time from sending a message until the answer comes back.
analogy: from posting a letter until the reply is in your mailbox.
precise: measured on one clock (the sender's), so it avoids synchronising two clocks; TCP measures it continuously to set its timers (F5-04).
source: D1 of F5-07 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1" (second edition), chapters on TCP data flow, window management and performance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much data arrives per second.
analogy: pages per day reaching your friend.
precise: bytes delivered to the receiving application per unit of time over an interval, limited by the slowest of link rate, window per round trip, CPU per byte and per call, and the application itself.
source: D1 of F5-07 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1" (second edition), chapters on TCP data flow, window management and performance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how slow the slowest few requests are.
analogy: the one letter in a hundred that takes a week.
precise: the high percentiles (99th, 99.9th) of a latency distribution; in systems where one user action waits for many requests, the tail decides what users feel.
source: D3 of F5-07 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (second edition), chapters on methodology, latency distributions and networks) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much data must be "on the wire" at once to keep a link busy.
analogy: how many pages must be on the road so your friend never waits for the next one.
precise: link rate × round-trip time; a sender must be allowed (by the receive window and the congestion window) at least this many unacknowledged bytes to reach the link rate.
source: D1 of F5-07 (W. Richard Stevens and Kevin R. Fall, "TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1" (second edition), chapters on TCP data flow, window management and performance) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a TCP rule that holds back small pieces of data while earlier data is unacknowledged, to send fewer tiny packets.
analogy: the clerk who holds your small note until the receipt for your last letter returns.
precise: if there is unacknowledged data in flight, a TCP sender buffers new data smaller than a full segment until an ACK arrives or a full segment accumulates; disabled per socket with the TCP_NODELAY option.
source: D5 of F5-07 (IETF RFC 1122, "Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers" (delayed ACKs; the Nagle algorithm)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a receiver waits a little before sending an ACK, hoping to send it together with reply data.
analogy: Amara waits to send the receipt until she writes back anyway.
precise: TCP receivers may delay a pure ACK for a short time (bounded by the standard) unless a second full segment arrives; combined with Nagle's algorithm on the other side it can stall request–response traffic until the delay timer fires.
source: D5 of F5-07 (IETF RFC 1122, "Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers" (delayed ACKs; the Nagle algorithm)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
